name: Thought & Knowledge
definition: Thought is the material response of memory, knowledge, and experience operating through the brain. Krishnamurti treats it as necessary in practical and technical matters but inherently limited in the psychological field, where it constructs the thinker as though separate from thinking, accumulates as the known, and perpetuates conflict through that division. Naming is one of its operations: 'the word is not the thing', and the description, the symbol, and the verbal association are mistaken for the actual — naming a state such as fear or anger can sustain the very reaction being named.
include_criteria: Include passages investigating thinking, memory, knowledge, experience, images, the thinker-thought division, or the proper and improper place of thought and the known; and passages examining the word versus the thing or fact, naming and its effect on perception, symbols and description, or how language conditions and obstructs seeing.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental references to having a thought or knowing a fact unless the passage examines thought's structure, limits, or psychological consequences.

aliases.alias: the word is not the thing

relations.note: Thought is the response of the conditioned past.
Thought creates the thinker as separate from thinking.

name: Conditioning
definition: Conditioning is the shaping of the mind by culture, tradition, religion, nationality, education, and accumulated experience, so that response arises from the past rather than from direct perception. Krishnamurti asks whether the conditioned mind can become aware of its own conditioning and be free of it, not gradually but through immediate seeing.
include_criteria: Include passages examining how the mind is programmed or shaped by society, culture, religion, propaganda, tradition, or the past, and whether one can be free of that shaping.
exclude_criteria: Exclude physical training or skill acquisition unless linked to psychological conditioning.

aliases.period_note: more frequent in later brain-focused talks and Bohm dialogues

relations.note: Conditioning operates as and through accumulated thought.
Freedom is freedom from conditioning.

name: Will, Effort & Escape
definition: Krishnamurti treats will as desire hardened into resolve — the self asserting itself as 'I will' or 'I will not' — and effort as the friction of that assertion against what is. Discipline, resistance, suppression, and the practice of a method are all its forms, and each strengthens the very self it is meant to overcome. Its mirror image is escape: the movement away from what is into entertainment, distraction, amusement, drink, ritual, or belief. Both are avoidance of the fact, and both cease not by a further act of will but in seeing the fact without the wish to change it.
include_criteria: Include passages examining will and 'I must', effort and struggle against oneself, discipline, control, suppression, resistance, or the practice of methods and systems; and passages examining escape, distraction, entertainment, and amusement as flight from what is.
exclude_criteria: Exclude ordinary physical effort or exertion, and casual uses of 'will' as a future tense. Route inquiry into conflict as such to conflict, and into order arising without discipline to order.

relations.note: Effort is conflict between what is and what should be.
Order comes from understanding disorder, not from discipline.
Will is the self asserting itself; seeing that is self-knowledge.
Escape is the movement away from what is.
Will operates in becoming — the gradual reaching of an ideal.

name: The Self ("the me")
definition: DEPRECATED 2026-07-25 — merged into 'self-knowledge' (Self-knowledge & The Self). All aliases and relations moved there. Retained as a tombstone so historical predictions keyed to this concept id stay resolvable.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the ego, the 'me' and 'mine', self-centred activity, self-importance, or the structure and ending of the self.
exclude_criteria: Exclude reflexive grammatical uses of 'self' and ordinary personal reference that do not examine the self as a psychological structure.

relations.note: Merged into Self-knowledge & The Self (2026-07-25).

name: Psychological Time & Becoming
definition: Beyond chronological time, Krishnamurti describes psychological time as the mind's movement from 'what is' toward 'what should be' — the becoming, achieving, and postponement by which thought avoids facing the present fact. This inward time is itself sorrow and fear; its ending is transformation now rather than gradual change. Chronological time is granted to the practical and is the necessary contrast, not a separate psychological root.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological time, becoming, the ideal versus the actual, gradualism, postponement, or 'tomorrow' as a psychological escape.
exclude_criteria: Exclude ordinary references to clock time, scheduling, or history unless used to illuminate psychological time.

relations.note: Becoming is gradual; mutation is immediate.
Time and becoming sustain sorrow.
Measurement against an ideal is the movement of becoming.

name: Relationship & Image-making
definition: Relationship is the mirror in which the self is revealed. Krishnamurti holds that we relate not to the person but to the image thought has made of them; these images divide people and produce conflict. To be related without images is a form of love and self-knowledge.
include_criteria: Include passages examining relationship as a mirror, image-making between people, dependence in relationship, or relating without the image.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental narrative mentions of people relating that do not examine relationship itself.

relations.note: Relationship is the field in which the self is seen.
Dependence and attachment corrupt relationship.

name: Division / Fragmentation
definition: Division is thought's fragmenting action: inner and outer, observer and observed, me and not-me, nationality and belief. Krishnamurti argues that psychological division breeds conflict and violence, and that wholeness is not the assembling of fragments but perception unbroken by the divider.
include_criteria: Include passages examining fragmentation, contradiction between fragments, the divider, or wholeness versus the broken-up mind.
exclude_criteria: Exclude neutral uses of 'division' (mathematical, organizational) with no psychological content.

aliases.period_note: the positive pole K names in later talks

relations.note: Division is the root of conflict.
'You are the world' — the individual/society division is illusory.

name: Belief & Ideals
definition: Belief, faith, ideology, and dogma are for Krishnamurti forms of psychological security that thought invents and that prevent seeing 'what is'. He regards belief as divisive and as a barrier to direct perception, whether it concerns God, the future, or a better self to become. (The ideal as 'what should be' belongs primarily to psychological time.)
include_criteria: Include passages examining belief, faith, ideology, dogma, or God-as-concept, especially as security or as an escape from fact.
exclude_criteria: Exclude casual uses of 'I believe' meaning 'I think' that do not treat belief as a structure; route the ideal-as-what-should-be to psychological time.

relations.note: Belief is a principal instrument of conditioning.
Belief in God differs from the discovery of the sacred.

name: Consciousness & Its Content
definition: Consciousness is its content — the whole field of thought, memory, fear, and conditioning shared by humankind. Because that content is common, 'you are the world': the individual is mankind, not separate from it. In his later work Krishnamurti sharpened a distinction between the conditioned brain and a mind not bound by the known; earlier he used brain and mind more interchangeably.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the nature and content of consciousness, the conscious and unconscious, the brain and its cells, the mind as distinct from the brain, or 'you are the world / the individual is mankind'.
exclude_criteria: Exclude casual uses of 'conscious of' or 'in mind' that do not examine consciousness, brain, or mind as such.

aliases.period_note: brain/mind distinction sharpened in 1970s-80s and the Bohm dialogues

relations.note: The content of consciousness is thought and its residue.
Mutation in the brain cells is K's later image of transformation.
Because consciousness is shared — you are the world — responsibility is total.

name: The Word & Naming
definition: DEPRECATED 2026-07-25 — folded into 'thought' (Thought & Knowledge). Its aliases and criteria moved there. Retained as a tombstone so historical predictions keyed to this concept id stay resolvable.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the word versus the thing or fact, naming and its effect on perception, symbols and description, or how language conditions and obstructs seeing.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental verbal or linguistic references that do not inquire into naming or the word-thing gap.

relations.note: Folded into Thought & Knowledge (2026-07-25).

name: Fear
definition: Fear is the psychological response produced when thought projects remembered pain or imagined danger into the future. In Krishnamurti's usage, it persists through time, avoidance, and the division between an observer and the feeling observed; the thought-and-time account is his principal analysis, and direct attention without that division is central to understanding it.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological fear, anxiety, insecurity, avoidance, or the operation of thought and time in sustaining fear.
exclude_criteria: Exclude purely practical responses to immediate physical danger and incidental uses of 'fear' that do not examine its nature or movement.

relations.note: Thought and psychological time often sustain fear by projecting remembered pain or future danger.
Fear and pleasure are two sides of the same movement of thought.

name: Desire & Pleasure
definition: Krishnamurti traces desire as the movement from perception to sensation to thought's image and pursuit, and pleasure as thought's demand to continue a sensation. Both are the counterpart of fear. He sets pursued pleasure against joy and bliss, which are uninvited and cannot be sought — joy belongs with love and the sacred, not with this mechanism.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the anatomy of desire, pleasure and its pursuit, gratification, sensation prolonged by thought, or sex as an expression of desire and pleasure.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental mentions of enjoying something with no examination of desire or pleasure; route joy/bliss as affirmation to love or the sacred.

relations.note: Pleasure and fear are the same movement of thought.
Desire hardens into attachment and dependence.

name: Suffering (Sorrow)
definition: Sorrow, for Krishnamurti, is not only personal grief but the sorrow of humankind, arising from self-concern, attachment, and thought's resistance to loss. He holds that remaining wholly with sorrow, without escape, ends it — and that the ending of sorrow is the beginning of compassion and wisdom.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological suffering, grief, self-pity, the sorrow of mankind, or the ending of sorrow.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental references to pain or misfortune that do not inquire into sorrow.

relations.note: The ending of sorrow is compassion.
Loneliness is a central form of sorrow.

name: Loneliness & Aloneness
definition: Loneliness is the ache of self-isolation and inner emptiness that thought and activity try to cover. Krishnamurti distinguishes it from aloneness — an uncorrupted, unconditioned state free of influence and dependence — which is discovered only when loneliness is fully faced rather than escaped.
include_criteria: Include passages examining loneliness, inner emptiness and escape from it, or the aloneness that is free of conditioning and dependence.
exclude_criteria: Exclude simple mentions of being physically alone with no psychological inquiry.

relations.note: Loneliness is a form of sorrow.
Escape from loneliness produces dependence.

name: Conflict
definition: Conflict is the friction of duality — between what is and what should be, desire and desire, the observer and the observed. Krishnamurti sees psychological conflict as unnecessary and rooted in division and comparison, and asks whether the mind can live wholly without inner struggle.
include_criteria: Include passages examining inner or outer conflict, struggle, effort born of contradiction, or living without conflict.
exclude_criteria: Exclude neutral descriptions of disputes or wars that do not inquire into the nature of conflict.

relations.note: Conflict springs from psychological division.
Unresolved conflict expresses itself as violence.

name: Violence
definition: Violence, for Krishnamurti, is far wider than physical harm: it includes anger, comparison, conformity, ambition, and the imitation of an ideal — including the ideal of non-violence. He holds that understanding the fact of one's own violence, without the ideal, is what ends it.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological violence, anger, aggression, brutality, conformity, or non-violence as an ideal.
exclude_criteria: Exclude mere reportage of violent events with no inquiry into violence itself; do not tag violence merely because ambition or comparison is mentioned unless violence is substantively at issue.

relations.note: Violence is conflict expressed.
K holds that all comparison is a form of violence.

name: Comparison & Measurement
definition: Psychological comparison — measuring oneself against another, against an ideal, against yesterday — is for Krishnamurti a root of becoming, envy, competition, conformity, and the sense of insufficiency; 'all comparison is violence.' Measurement is the mind's instrument, and the immeasurable is precisely what lies beyond it.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological comparison, inward measurement, envy or competition born of comparison, 'the more', conformity to an ideal, or measurement contrasted with the immeasurable.
exclude_criteria: Exclude practical, scientific, or technical measurement unless explicitly contrasted with psychological measurement.

relations.note: Comparison is the measuring that drives becoming.
K holds that all comparison is violence.
The measure versus the immeasurable.

name: Security & Attachment
definition: The craving for psychological security drives attachment — to people, beliefs, possessions, and self-images — and Krishnamurti shows that attachment breeds fear, dependence, jealousy, and sorrow. Detachment is only its opposite and equally bound; freedom lies in understanding the demand for security itself.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological security and insecurity, attachment, dependence, possessiveness, jealousy, or the cultivated ideal of detachment.
exclude_criteria: Exclude references to physical or financial security that do not touch psychological dependence.

relations.note: The search for security is driven by fear.
Attachment corrupts relationship into dependence.

name: Authority & Following
definition: Krishnamurti rejects spiritual and psychological authority — gurus, saviours, systems, and the authority of one's own accumulated experience — as incompatible with the discovery of truth. 'Truth is a pathless land'; following another only conforms the mind and prevents self-knowledge.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological or spiritual authority, gurus and disciples, following, obedience, tradition-as-authority, or the authority of experience.
exclude_criteria: Exclude references to practical or legal authority (expertise, law) that do not touch psychological following.

relations.note: Freedom requires the ending of psychological authority.
Only self-knowledge, not authority, uncovers truth.

name: Freedom
definition: Freedom is not choice, permissiveness, or movement toward an ideal; it is freedom from psychological conditioning, authority, fear, and the known. In Krishnamurti's usage it is present at the beginning of inquiry rather than awarded at its end, and arises with direct perception of conditioning rather than through effort or gradual achievement.
include_criteria: Include passages examining inward freedom, liberation from conditioning or authority, or why freedom must be immediate and not an eventual reward.
exclude_criteria: Exclude merely political, legal, or physical liberty unless the passage explicitly connects it to psychological freedom.

relations.note: Freedom is freedom from conditioning.
Freedom is incompatible with psychological authority.

name: The Observer Is the Observed
definition: Krishnamurti's central perceptual discovery: the thinker is the thought, the experiencer the experience, the observer the observed. The division between the one who watches and the thing watched is created by thought; when it is seen that they are one movement, conflict and the effort to control dissolve.
include_criteria: Include passages where the observer-observed identity claim is substantive: the thinker and the thought, the experiencer and experience, or the collapse of that division in perception.
exclude_criteria: Exclude ordinary uses of 'observe' or 'notice', and general talk of awareness, that do not assert the observer-observed identity.

relations.note: The observer is the self set apart by thought.
Choiceless awareness is observation without the observer.

name: Awareness & Attention
definition: Awareness is choiceless observation — inward and outward — without judgement, condemnation, or the effort of concentration. Krishnamurti distinguishes attention, a total unfragmented seeing free of a centre, from concentration, which is exclusion and resistance. In such attention the observer is absent.
include_criteria: Include passages examining choiceless awareness, attention versus concentration, observing without judgement, or the quality of attention itself.
exclude_criteria: Exclude casual uses of 'aware' or 'pay attention'; route inquiry into 'what is' versus 'what should be' to truth, not here.

relations.note: In full attention the observer is the observed.
Choiceless awareness is the ground of meditation.
Listening is choiceless awareness in the field of hearing.

name: Listening
definition: Krishnamurti treats listening as an art in its own right: to hear without the screen of opinion, conclusion, agreement, or the running commentary of comparison with what one already knows. Most hearing is interpretation — the mind translating what is said into its own terms — and so nothing new enters. In listening completely, without effort or resistance, the thing said is seen rather than argued with, and that seeing is itself the action.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the art of listening, hearing without interpretation or conclusion, listening to another or to oneself, or the difference between hearing words and listening completely.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental uses of 'listen' or 'hear' — stage directions, requests for quiet, references to listening to the radio or to music — that do not inquire into the quality of listening itself.

relations.note: Listening is choiceless awareness in the field of hearing.
Learning begins with listening without a conclusion.
Interpretation while listening is thought intervening.

name: Insight & Intelligence
definition: Insight is direct, immediate perception of truth that is not the conclusion of thought, memory, or analysis; Krishnamurti holds that seeing the false as false is itself the action that frees. Intelligence, distinct from mere intellect or cleverness, is the sensitivity and clarity that flowers when thought is in its right place.
include_criteria: Include passages examining insight, immediate perception, seeing-is-acting, or intelligence as distinct from intellect, knowledge, and cleverness.
exclude_criteria: Exclude ordinary uses of 'intelligent' or 'insightful' that do not inquire into their nature.

relations.note: In insight the seeing is the doing.
Insight is not the movement of thought.

name: Learning & Education
definition: Learning, for Krishnamurti, is a living movement of observing and understanding, not the accumulation of knowledge to be stored and repeated. Right education awakens intelligence and self-knowledge and frees the mind from fear and conformity, rather than merely training it for a career or shaping it to society.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the art of learning versus accumulating knowledge, education and its true function, teaching, the right relationship of student and teacher, or awakening intelligence in the young.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental references to schools or facts learned that do not inquire into learning or education.

relations.note: Learning begins in the art of listening and seeing without accumulation.
True learning awakens intelligence.

name: Truth & "What Is"
definition: Krishnamurti holds that truth is a pathless land, to be discovered directly and never through belief, authority, or method — it is not produced by thought. Understanding begins with facing 'what is', the actual fact, without escape into 'what should be'; the fact, observed without distortion, undergoes its own transformation. He sometimes uses 'reality' for what thought constructs, in contrast to truth.
include_criteria: Include passages examining truth and how it is or is not found, actuality, 'what is' versus 'what should be', or staying with the fact.
exclude_criteria: Exclude casual uses of 'true' or 'in fact', and do not treat 'reality' as a synonym for truth where the passage means thought's construction.

relations.note: 'What should be' is the escape from 'what is' into time.
Truth cannot be reached through another's authority.

name: Order & Disorder
definition: Order, for Krishnamurti, is not imposed discipline, conformity, or a blueprint, but the natural outcome of understanding disorder in oneself. Discipline is the act of learning, not suppression or control; virtue and order flower when the causes of inner disorder — conflict, contradiction, fear — are seen.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological order and disorder, discipline as learning versus control, virtue, or how order arises from understanding disorder.
exclude_criteria: Exclude neutral references to tidiness, sequence, or rules that do not inquire into inner order.

relations.note: Disorder is the inner conflict that order resolves.
True discipline is inseparable from freedom, not opposed to it.

name: Action
definition: Krishnamurti examines action that springs from an idea, ideal, or conclusion — always incomplete and productive of conflict — versus action that is the immediate expression of perception, where the seeing and the doing are one. Complete action leaves no residue of regret or division.
include_criteria: Include passages examining action and idea, complete versus fragmentary action, right action, doing without motive, or the gap between seeing and acting.
exclude_criteria: Exclude ordinary narrative uses of 'action' or 'do' that do not inquire into the nature of action.

relations.note: In insight the seeing is the doing.
Action from an ideal defers into time.

name: Self-knowledge & The Self
definition: Self-knowledge is for Krishnamurti the foundation of all understanding: the ceaseless observation of oneself in the mirror of relationship, moment to moment, without accumulating a conclusion about oneself. What is known in it — the self, the 'me', the ego — is a bundle of memories, images, and wants built by thought, not a permanent entity; it divides itself from others and from experience and is the root of psychological conflict. Knowing and the thing known are one movement here: the ending of the self is not achieved by another effort of the self, but comes with seeing it whole.
include_criteria: Include passages examining self-knowledge, knowing oneself, reading 'the book of oneself', or observing the self in relationship without a conclusion; and passages examining the ego, the 'me' and 'mine', self-centred activity, self-importance, or the structure and ending of the self.
exclude_criteria: Exclude introspection aimed at self-improvement, references to personality traits that do not inquire into self-knowing, reflexive grammatical uses of 'self', and ordinary personal reference that does not examine the self as a psychological structure.

relations.note: The self is known only in the mirror of relationship.
The self is the central divider.
The self is the content of consciousness.

name: Love & Compassion
definition: Krishnamurti approaches love by negation — it is not desire, pleasure, attachment, jealousy, dependence, or the image thought builds. What remains when these end is love, inseparable from compassion and intelligence; compassion arises with the ending of sorrow and the self. Joy is its natural note, not something to be pursued.
include_criteria: Include passages examining what love is and is not, compassion, tenderness, joy as affirmation, or the distinction of love from attachment, desire, and jealousy.
exclude_criteria: Exclude casual uses of 'love' (liking, preference) that do not inquire into its nature.

relations.note: Compassion arises with the ending of sorrow.
Love is not attachment or dependence.

name: Death & Ending
definition: Krishnamurti treats death not as a distant event to fear but as ending — the dying each day to memory, attachment, and the known. To live and die from moment to moment, with nothing carried over, is to meet life afresh; living and dying are then one indivisible movement.
include_criteria: Include passages where death, the fear of death, ending and the known, dying to each day, or the relationship of living and dying is the central inquiry.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental mentions of someone dying, and do not tag every psychological ending as death unless death, continuity, or dying to the known is substantively at issue.

relations.note: Fear of death is thought's continuity resisting ending.
Dying to the known is a form of freedom.

name: Meditation & Silence
definition: For Krishnamurti meditation is not a method, practice, mantra, or system — all of which condition the mind — but the emptying of consciousness of the known, out of which comes a silence not induced by thought. It cannot be pursued or achieved; it is the whole movement of a mind free of the self.
include_criteria: Include passages examining meditation, its false and true forms, silence and stillness of the mind, systems and mantras, or the meditative mind.
exclude_criteria: Exclude references to concentration techniques or relaxation that the passage does not connect to meditation as K means it.

relations.note: Choiceless awareness is the ground of meditation.
In the silence of meditation the sacred may be.

name: Beauty
definition: Beauty, for Krishnamurti, is not merely in the object, the picture, or the poem but in a state of mind free of the self — where, in the presence of a mountain or great beauty, the 'me' is momentarily absent. It is inseparable from sensitivity, love, and austerity, and cannot be cultivated.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the nature of beauty, sensitivity to beauty, the absence of the self in the presence of beauty, or beauty's relation to love and austerity.
exclude_criteria: Exclude incidental descriptions of beautiful things that do not inquire into beauty.

relations.note: Beauty and love are inseparable.
In the perception of beauty the self is absent.

name: Nature & the Earth
definition: Krishnamurti's relationship with nature — the mountains, trees, rivers, light, and living things — pervades his talks and writings as a doorway to sensitivity and the absence of the self. He held that losing touch with nature is losing touch with oneself and with humanity, and that care for the earth is inseparable from the teaching.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the observation of nature, the beauty and order of the earth, our relationship with living things, or sensitivity to nature as a way of seeing.
exclude_criteria: Exclude passing scene-setting mentions of weather or landscape that carry no inquiry.

relations.note: Nature is a doorway to beauty and the absence of the self.
In deep attention to nature the self recedes.

name: Energy & Passion
definition: Krishnamurti speaks of the energy dissipated in conflict, fear, and the self, and of the undivided energy released when those wastages end — an energy needed for transformation and for meditation. Passion, distinct from lust or enthusiasm for a cause, is the intensity that comes with the ending of sorrow and total attention.
include_criteria: Include passages examining psychological energy, its dissipation and gathering, passion as intensity (not lust), or the energy required for transformation and attention.
exclude_criteria: Exclude references to physical or physiological energy that carry no psychological inquiry.

relations.note: K says the root of passion is sorrow.
Undivided energy is needed for mutation.

name: Transformation & Mutation
definition: Krishnamurti calls for a radical transformation — total and immediate, not the gradual reform of becoming — that alone can end humanity's inherited disorder. In his earlier decades he framed this as the 'only revolution', which is inward; in the later dialogues he spoke of a mutation of the mind and even of the brain cells (his own formulation, not a neurological claim).
include_criteria: Include passages examining radical inward transformation, mutation, regeneration, the 'only revolution', or immediate change versus gradual becoming.
exclude_criteria: Exclude political, social, or economic revolution unless explicitly contrasted with inward transformation.

aliases.period_note: brain-cell phrasing prominent in later talks and Bohm dialogues

relations.note: Mutation is immediate; becoming is gradual.
Insight is the instrument of mutation.

name: The Religious Mind & the Sacred
definition: The religious mind, for Krishnamurti, has nothing to do with organized religion, belief, ritual, or authority. It is a mind that is free, without fear, in a state of inquiry and negation, that has understood itself — and only such a mind may come upon what he points to, always by negation, as the sacred: something nameless and immeasurable that may be when the mind is empty of the self and of thought — 'that benediction', 'the otherness', the timeless. It cannot be sought, named, or held, and is not the God of belief.
include_criteria: Include passages examining the religious mind or spirit, true versus organized religion, the quality of a mind in religious inquiry, negation as the approach to the religious, or passages pointing to the sacred, the immeasurable, the nameless, the timeless, benediction, bliss/ecstasy as the uninvited, or 'the otherness'.
exclude_criteria: Exclude descriptive references to churches, rituals, or religious institutions that do not inquire into the religious mind, and uses of 'sacred' or 'holy' tied to religious tradition or belief that the passage does not transcend.

relations.note: The religious mind is free of belief and organized religion.
In the silence of meditation the sacred may be.

name: The Sacred / The Immeasurable
definition: DEPRECATED 2026-07-16 — merged into 'religious-mind' (The Religious Mind & the Sacred). All aliases and relations moved there; slot reused for the new 'responsibility' root. Retained as a tombstone so historical predictions keyed to this concept id stay resolvable.
include_criteria: Include passages pointing to the sacred, the immeasurable, the nameless, the timeless, benediction, bliss/ecstasy as the uninvited, or 'the otherness' — approached through negation.
exclude_criteria: Exclude uses of 'sacred' or 'holy' tied to religious tradition or belief that the passage does not transcend.

relations.note: Merged into The Religious Mind & the Sacred (2026-07-16).

name: Responsibility
definition: For Krishnamurti responsibility is total, not partial: because your consciousness is the consciousness of mankind — 'you are the world' — you are responsible for the whole of it: for the wars, for society, for the education of children, for the earth. It is not duty, guilt, or obligation but the ability to respond wholly to what is, out of relationship rather than out of ideals.
include_criteria: Include passages on being responsible for the whole (society, war, the earth), 'you are the world, you are responsible', the responsibility of parents and educators, responsibility in relationship, or responsibility as complete response to what is.
exclude_criteria: Exclude passing practical or organizational uses of 'responsible'/'duty' that the passage does not examine psychologically.

relations.note: Total responsibility rests on shared consciousness — you are the world.
Responsibility is lived in relationship; society is its projection.
Responsibility as the ability to respond to what is, without the gap of ideals.
'You are responsible for every war' — his most frequent concrete use.
The responsibility of the educator and parent, central in the school talks.
